extracted.intended_audience: architects, architectural historians, restorers, and informed readers of architectural criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and critical criteria for designing, judging, and restoring Venetian (especially ecclesiastical) architecture — covering proportions, ornament, placement of fittings (pulpits), shafts/columns, material use, and honesty of construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and refined adaptation of elements
rubrics_metrics.description: 'the delicate adaptation of this diminished base to the diminished shaft is a piece of fastidiousness in proportion' — subtle proportional adjustments (even when not obvious from crude outlines) are a virtue and should be detected and appreciated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when bases or other mouldings appear rude in contour, fine proportional refinements (for perspective or visual harmony) are important. Architects and critics should look for small modifications that harmonize adjoining parts (e.g., diminishing bases/shafts in more distant pillars to support perspective).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulpit ornamentation must have grace, meaning, and tasteful relation to the church
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is no character of an ordinary modern English church which appears to me more to be regretted than the peculiar pompousness of the furniture of the pulpits' — pulpit furniture should not be pompous, meaningless, or merely upholstery-driven, especially when the rest of the church is meagre in color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid excessive upholstery and ostentatious decoration on pulpits that clashes with or overwhelms the rest of the interior. Furnishings should have coherence with the church's overall palette and meaning, and should not be independent showy objects without grace.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pulpit placement should respect liturgical function and acoustics (primitive arrangement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The primitive (and often preferable) arrangement has the preacher in the centre of the apse/throne area; lateral pulpits are of later date and often poorer for original function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider historical precedent and acoustic performance: Bunsen found the voice is heard more plainly from the centre of the apse than from other spots. Therefore pulpit position must balance liturgical sanctity (eastern extremity reserved for communion) with practical concerns (audibility), and restorations or new work should favor positions consonant with primitive practice when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preaching practice and decorum at the pulpit
rubrics_metrics.description: Criticism of the habit of making a desk of the Bible and 'reading the sermon stealthily' — using the Scriptures as a cover for notes is unseemly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While debates exist over extemporization vs. memorization, ministers should avoid disguising notes as Scripture consultation. Ritual strictness that forces unnecessary memorization may have unintended unseemly consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation and adjustment of bases for continuous Gothic effect
rubrics_metrics.description: When closely adjacent square plinths leave an awkward fissure, the architect may cut parts away and fit them close together, producing a continuous Gothic base (early Venetian instance).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical adjustment of mouldings and bases to avoid awkward gaps (even if it requires cutting mouldings) is acceptable when it yields a continuous, harmonious aggregation of shafts. This demonstrates an early Gothic principle of aggregation and continuous base design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate proportions, tapering, and spacing of shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific proportional practice: shafts measured (example) ~2 ft. 8½ in. circumference at base, tapering to 2 ft. under the lowest fillet in 5 ft. 6 in. height; nearest spacing as little as 2½ in., about 5 in. at necks of capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shafts should be proportioned and tapered in measured relation to their height and to each other; close spacing and delicate curvature can be intentional expressive devices. Use measured proportion as a guide to visual harmony and constructive logic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place shafts near a backing wall to best display material and color
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting pillars within two or three inches of a sheeted wall forms a grove effect and brings out the shaft's color and quality; the wall provides a sharp shadow that intensifies the shaft's colors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design to exploit sunlight and shadow: bringing a broad wall surface close behind a shaft produces sharp, dark shadows that increase color brilliance; in overcast conditions the subdued wall veil gives subtle half-shadows equally advantageous. Consider light interplay when locating and mounting shafts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honesty in structural expression (do not pretend work the shafts do not actually perform)
rubrics_metrics.description: The builder avoids 'dishonesty' by visibly leaving many shafts with half their capitals projecting beyond the archivolts they sustain, showing the wall is only slightly dependent on them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not feign structural responsibility in shafts or ornaments. If a shaft is not carrying the full load, architectural expression should honestly show that (e.g., leaving capitals projecting) rather than implying a false structural role by deceptive forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate sizing and superimposition of shafts (follow natural laws)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use largest shafts for nave, smaller for windows/jambs etc.; middle-sized shafts sorted into two classes with upper series smaller and more numerous; proper subdivided superimposition (upper shafts diminish in size and multiply) is the correct practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shafts should be allocated by function and position — largest where strength/importance required, smaller where decorative or for lighter service. Superimposition should diminish and increase number upwards (as in trees), not merely stack identical shafts; this follows natural laws and constructive sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid gratuitous or purely theoretical small subsidiary shafts
rubrics_metrics.description: Critique of small 'satellitic' shafts introduced without sufficient reason (e.g., early English piers) which have nothing but delicacy and theoretical connection to recommend them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not introduce small subsidiary shafts purely for ornament without functional or expressive justification; such additions may be 'gratuitous' unless they genuinely contribute to constructive balance or aesthetic purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance and poise as the basis of stability (not mere breadth of foundation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain angular portico compositions rely on accuracy of poise rather than breadth/strength of foundation: 'It is a balanced, not a propped structure: if the balance fails, it must fall instantly; if the balance is maintained, no matter how the lower shaft is fastened into the ground, all will be safe.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design systems that achieve equilibrium through correct disposition of weights and proportions; bases and plinth forms may be adapted (circular base sustaining hexagonal plinth obliquely) to indicate and secure balance. Read the ground plan to see how balance is achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Let materials determine the aims of the art (honour material capabilities)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'All art, working with given materials, must propose to itself the objects which, with those materials, are most perfectly attainable; and becomes illegitimate and debased if it propose to itself any other objects, better attainable with other materials.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not force a material to express effects it cannot do well; for instance, avoid carving extremely intricate, filamentary structures (like birds' nests) in marble when painting can render them perfectly. Limit detail in sculpture to what can be 'with perfect ease represented' in the material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workman should bring out and exalt peculiar qualities of material
rubrics_metrics.description: 'The workman ... should insist upon and exhibit [marble's] transparency and solidity; if in iron, its strength and tenacity; if in gold, its ductility.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When designing or crafting, highlight and exploit the intrinsic virtues of the chosen material (marble's translucency, iron's strength, gold's ductility). The material will be 'grateful' and the result more truthful and beautiful.
